title: Approach to the Patient With CNS Infection

questions.question: Cerebrospinal fluid chemistries.
questions.question_raw:
Q1 (2008) CSF Chemistries
What are 3 differential diagnoses of hypoglycorrhacia other than acute bacterial meningitis?

parts.text: What are 3 differential diagnoses of hypoglycorrhachia other than acute bacterial meningitis?

parts_raw.text: What are 3 differential diagnoses of hypoglycorrhacia other than acute bacterial meningitis?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Tuberculous meningitis (CSF glucose typically <45 mg/dL). (2) Cryptococcal/fungal meningitis (glucose <40 mg/dL). (3) Carcinomatous (neoplastic) meningitis. Hypoglycorrhachia is multifactorial (increased glycolysis by leukocytes/bacteria, increased CNS metabolic rate, impaired membrane glucose transport) and is not specific to acute bacterial meningitis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Carcinomatous/neoplastic meningitis as a cause of low CSF glucose is standard teaching (not explicitly listed in this chapter, which tabulates tuberculous and cryptococcal causes).

cohort_answer.text:
Fungal meningitis
TB meningitis
Amoebic meningitis/meningoencephalitis
Viral meningitis (esp in children – eg enterovirus)

questions.question: Drug penetration into cerebrospinal fluid.

parts.text: List 2 (or 4) factors that influence drug penetration into CSF.

parts_raw.text: List 2 (or 4) factors that influence drug penetration into CSF

questions.model_answer: a) Entry of an antimicrobial into CSF is enhanced by: (1) low molecular weight; (2) low degree of ionization at physiologic pH; (3) high lipid solubility; (4) low degree of protein binding. Penetration also depends on the status of the blood-brain barrier, which is disrupted (increasing entry) by meningeal inflammation.

cohort_answer.text: Better penetration with: low molecular weight; high lipid solubility; low degree of protein binding; low degree of ionization at physiologic pH (better penetration in unionized form); meningeal inflammation.
